Quantum Electron Quasicrystal

Pierre-Antoine Graham Affiliation: Department of Physics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA-02139, USA    Filippo Gaggioli Affiliation: Department of Physics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA-02139, USA    Liang Fu Affiliation: Department of Physics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA-02139, USA
August 24, 2026
Abstract

The strongly correlated phases of the homogeneous electron gas constitute the vocabulary of many-body condensed matter physics and find a natural realization in semiconductors. In this setting, recent neural-network variational Monte Carlo calculations [1] discovered an unexpected quantum phase of matter in wide quantum wells: an electronic quasicrystal formed by a bilayer Wigner crystals with a 30∘30^{\circ} twist. This state defies classical expectations and emerges in a regime dominated by quantum fluctuations. Here, we develop an analytical framework to reveal its origin. By computing zero-point energy corrections to bilayer Wigner crystal configurations, we show that quantum fluctuations qualitatively reshape the energetic landscape, destabilizing the classical honeycomb state and selecting the 30∘30^{\circ} quasicrystalline ground state over a broad parameter range. Our results identify zero-point motion as the mechanism stabilizing the electronic quasicrystal and establish a route to spontaneous moiré physics driven by many-body quantum effects.

The competition between energy and entropy gives rise to a rich variety of phases of matter as a function of temperature. Atoms arrange into crystalline solids that minimize interaction energy, form liquids when thermal fluctuations dominate, and can even realize quasicrystalline order when competing interactions favor non-periodic structures [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7].

In quantum systems, the uncertainty in electron’s position leads to a competition between localized and itinerant electron phases. For electrons at zero temperature, quantum fluctuations produce quantum liquids such as metals, while strong Coulomb interaction drives electron crystals [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13], first predicted long ago by Wigner [14]. Yet, the nature of quantum melting and possible phases that can emerge in its vicinity remain open questions [15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21]. In particular, whether there exists quantum analogues of quasicrystals in electronic systems is an outstanding problem.

Semiconductor quantum wells provide a particularly versatile setting in which to explore these questions. In the two-dimensional limit, the competition between interaction and kinetic energy gives rise to a transition from a metallic state to a triangular Wigner crystal at low electron densities. Confinement in the transverse direction introduces an additional degree of freedom, allowing the electron gas to access both monolayer and bilayer regimes [22, 10] and enriching the landscape of competing ground states. The interplay of energy scales stabilizes a variety of crystalline phases [23, 24, 25] and offers a controlled platform for probing quantum melting.

Recently, this problem has been revisited using neural-network-based variational Monte Carlo (NN-VMC), which enables unbiased simulations of interacting electrons in continuous space [26, 27]. In a previous work [1], we uncovered a rich phase diagram of electrons in wide quantum wells, including both monolayer and bilayer Wigner crystals. Most strikingly, in the bilayer regime near the onset of quantum melting, we discovered a previously unknown quantum phase of matter: an electron quasicrystal formed by a 30∘30^{\circ}-twist between two layers of triangular Wigner crystals.

This quasicrystalline state defies classical expectations. In a purely classical bilayer of point charges, the ground state is known to favor crystalline configurations, such as a honeycomb structure. By contrast, the quasicrystal we identified emerges in a regime where quantum fluctuations are strong and fundamentally alter the energetic hierarchy of competing states. Its stability therefore has no classical analogue and instead originates from zero-point motion of the electrons. This establishes the electronic quasicrystal as a genuinely quantum phase of matter.

In this work, we develop an analytical theory to reveal the quantum origin and stability of the emergent quasicrystal phase in electronic bilayer systems. Our approach is based on quantifying the zero-point energy of collective fluctuations around candidate bilayer configurations, for arbitrary twist angles.

Our analysis reveals that quantum fluctuations qualitatively reshape the phase diagram of bilayer electron systems. While classical energetics favor the honeycomb configuration, we show that sufficiently strong zero-point motion stabilizes twisted electronic structures. Among these, the 30∘30^{\circ} twisted configuration—corresponding to a quasicrystalline arrangement—is found to minimize the total energy and thus emerges as the true ground state in a broad parameter regime. These results provide a transparent physical explanation for the numerical observations of NN-VMC and establish zero-point fluctuations as the key mechanism driving the formation of the electronic quasicrystal.

Classical ground state – We consider a bilayer system of spin-polarized electrons with density n2​Dn_{2D} and interparticle distance rs=(πn2​D)−1/2r_{s}=(\pi n_{2D})^{-1/2}, with two layers l=1,2l=1,2 with separation tst_{s} and of equal density n2​D/2n_{2D}/2 as shown in Fig. 1 (a). Note the difference between rsr_{s} and the usual definition involving the density of a single layer given by rsmono=2​rsr_{s}^{\rm mono}=\sqrt{2}r_{s}. Unless stated otherwise, we use the effective Hartree system ℏ=e=m=aB=1\hbar=e=m=a_{B}=1 where mm is the effective electron mass and aBa_{B} the effective Bohr radius. The effective Hartree energy is EH=ℏ2/m​aB2E_{\rm H}=\hbar^{2}/ma_{B}^{2}.

We denote the position of an electron ii in layer ℓ\ell as 𝐫i,ℓ=(𝝆i,ℓ,zi,ℓ)\mathbf{r}_{i,\ell}=(\bm{\rho}_{i,\ell},z_{i,\ell}) with zi,1=−ts/2z_{i,1}=-t_{s}/2 and zi,2=ts/2z_{i,2}=t_{s}/2. The Hamiltonian of Coulomb interacting electrons then reads

H\displaystyle H =−12∑i,ℓ(∇i,ℓ2+∑≠i,ℓ1|𝝆i,ℓ−𝝆j,ℓ′|2+δℓ≠ℓ′​ts2)\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,\ell}\!\left(\nabla_{i,\ell}^{2}+\sum_{\neq i,\ell}\!\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\bm{\rho}_{i,\ell}\!-\!\bm{\rho}_{j,\ell^{\prime}}|^{2}+\delta_{\ell\neq\ell^{\prime}}\,t_{s}^{2}}}\right) (1)

up to the interaction with a neutralizing background. As we will show later, Equation (1) captures the essential physics of the bilayer regime that spontaneously occurs in semiconductor wide quantum wells [1]. For large values of rsr_{s}, interactions dominate over the kinetic energy and the ground state of the Hamiltonian (1) is an electron crystal. In particular, for large values of ts/rst_{s}/r_{s}, intralayer Coulomb energy dominates over interlayer interaction, and therefore electrons on each layer form a triangular Wigner crystal.

In this work, we study the twist angle θ\theta dependence of the energy of such bilayer stackings. To start, we focus on the classical Coulomb interaction energy per particle uu, which scales ∝1/rs\propto 1/r_{s} at fixed ts/rst_{s}/r_{s}. It consists of intralayer terms for each layer, which are minimized by a triangular lattice geometry, and an interlayer term that reads

uinter=π​n2​D2​∑𝐆≠𝟎e−|𝐆|​ts|𝐆|​ρ1​(𝐆)​ρ2​(−𝐆),\displaystyle u_{\rm inter}=\frac{\pi n_{\rm 2D}}{2}\sum_{\mathbf{G}\neq\mathbf{0}}\frac{e^{-|\mathbf{G}|t_{s}}}{|\mathbf{G}|}\rho_{1}(\mathbf{G})\rho_{2}(-\mathbf{G}), (2)

where ρℓ​(𝐆)=2N​∑iei​𝐆⋅𝝆i,ℓ\rho_{\ell}(\mathbf{G})=\frac{2}{N}\sum_{i}e^{i\mathbf{G}\cdot\bm{\rho}_{i,\ell}} the Fourier components of the charge density in layer ℓ\ell for NN electrons. Equation (2) favors commensurate stackings: the product ρℓ​(𝐆)​ρℓ′​(−𝐆)∝ei​𝐆⋅𝐬\rho_{\ell}(\mathbf{G})\rho_{\ell^{\prime}}(-\mathbf{G})\propto e^{i\mathbf{G}\cdot\mathbf{s}} is generically non-zero, and since ∫d2​𝐬​uinter​(𝐬)=0\int\text{d}^{2}\mathbf{s}\,\,u_{\rm inter}(\mathbf{s})=0 there must exist a shift 𝐬\mathbf{s} that lowers energy relative to the decoupled limit value uinter=0u_{\rm inter}=0. On the other hand, uinteru_{\rm inter} vanishes if there is no common Fourier density components.

For a rigid bilayer at sufficiently large ts/rst_{s}/r_{s}, the honeycomb configuration (θ=0\theta=0) minimizes the interlayer energy (2), which reads

uinter∼−πn2​De−G​ts/G,u_{\text{inter}}\sim-\pi\,n_{2D}\,e^{-Gt_{s}}/G, (3)

with G=4​π/3​a∼rs−1G=4\pi/\sqrt{3}a\sim r_{s}^{-1} and aa the lattice constant of the triangular layers. For twisted rigid bilayers, on the other hand, we find that the interlayer energy is negligible even for commensurate stackings, as shown by the red line in Fig. 1 (c).

In a realistic bilayer, however, electrons in each layer experience interlayer forces and relax toward a (local) energy minimum that deviates from the rigid triangular lattice. In order to obtain mechanically stable configurations at different twist angles, we start from two triangular layers and use gradient descent to minimize the classical Coulomb energy.

Similarly to other twisted bilayers [29, 30, 31], relaxation creates a modulation with characteristic lengthscale LM=a2​sin⁡(θ/2)∼|𝐆1−𝐆2|−1L_{M}=\frac{a}{2\sin(\theta/2)}\sim|\mathbf{G}_{1}-\mathbf{G}_{2}|^{-1} that imprints common ρl​(𝐆l′)\rho_{l}(\mathbf{G}_{l^{\prime}}) components in each layer, thus lowering the interlayer energy (2). This comes at the expenses of an intralayer elastic energy cost κ​(δ​r/LM)2\kappa(\delta r/L_{M})^{2}, with δ​r\delta r being the typical displacement and κ∼a−1\kappa\sim a^{-1} the relevant elastic constant. At small angles, LM≫1L_{M}\gg 1 and the elastic energy cost is negligible, thus leading to strong relaxation. On the other hand, the elastic energy becomes comparable to uinter∼n2​D​e−G​ts/Gu_{\rm inter}\sim n_{2D}e^{-Gt_{s}}/G for twist angles

sin2⁡(θ/2)≳e−G​ts/κ​a∝e−G​ts,\sin^{2}(\theta/2)\gtrsim e^{-Gt_{s}}/\kappa\,a\propto e^{-Gt_{s}}, (4)

beyond which the effect of relaxation is weak. Balancing the elastic and interlayer forces in the large angle limit, κ​δ​r/LM2∼e−G​ts/a2\kappa\,\delta r/L_{M}^{2}\sim e^{-Gt_{s}}/a^{2}, we then find typical displacements of order δ​r∼LM2​e−G​ts/a\delta r\sim L_{M}^{2}e^{-Gt_{s}}/a and, correspondingly, the classical energy is lowered by

u⁡(θ)∼e−2​G​ts/a​sin2⁡(θ/2),u(\theta)\sim e^{-2Gt_{s}}/a\sin^{2}(\theta/2), (5)

as detailed in Section III of the SM [32].

The classical energies after relaxation are shown in blue in Fig. 1 (c) for ts/rs=3t_{s}/r_{s}=3. These energies were using the adapted Ewald summation method [33, 24] obtained for commensurate twist angles where the moiré pattern exactly repeats as a superlattice (see Sec. I of the SM [32] for more details) – the smoothness of the angular dependence then allows to extrapolate to the neighboring incommensurate configurations. In particular, we can always find a family of commensurate approximants that converge towards a given incommensurate stacking. Comparing to the numerics, we find that our analytical scaling (5) (orange dashed) reproduces the classical energy u⁡(θ)u(\theta) over a wide range of twist angles angles, for sufficiently large values of ts/rst_{s}/r_{s}.

At the classical level, we have therefore found that relaxation plays an important role, but makes the honeycomb stacking and quasicrystal stackings as the lowest and highest energy configurations, respectively. This picture will change upon including the effect of quantum fluctuations, as we will now show below.

Zero-point energy – Quantum fluctuations modify the stability of classical configurations by means of the zero-point energy contribution ZPE=∑iℏ​ωi/2\text{ZPE}=\sum_{i}\hbar\omega_{i}/2 from their collective excitations. To calculate the ZPE as a function of twist angle, we consider small displacements of an electron α,l\alpha,l around the classical relaxed configuration,

𝐮𝐑​α​ℓ=1Ncell​∑𝐪𝜸𝐪​α​ℓ​ei​𝐪⋅𝐑,\displaystyle\mathbf{u}_{\mathbf{R}\alpha\ell}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{\rm cell}}}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}\bm{\gamma}_{\mathbf{q}\alpha\ell}\,e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}}, (6)

where 𝐑\mathbf{R} is the superlattice site and NcellN_{\text{cell}} is the number of repeating supercells in the bilayer stacking [32]. The wave-vector 𝐪\mathbf{q} belongs to the mini-Brillouin zone of the superlattice, which reduces to a single point 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 in the case of an incommensurate stacking formed by a single, infinitely large, supercell.

Rewriting the Hamiltonian (1) in terms of the displacements 𝐮𝐑​α​ℓ\mathbf{u}_{\mathbf{R}\alpha\ell} and expanding to quadratic order in 𝜸𝐪​α​ℓ\bm{\gamma}_{\mathbf{q}\alpha\ell}, we obtain the coupled-harmonic oscillator problem

H=−12\displaystyle H=-\frac{1}{2} ∑𝐑​α​ℓ∇𝐑​α​ℓ2+12​∑𝐪​α​ℓ​β​ℓ′𝜸𝐪​β​ℓ′†​𝐃α​βℓ​ℓ′​(𝐪)​𝜸𝐪​α​ℓ,\displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{R}\alpha\ell}\nabla_{\mathbf{R}\alpha\ell}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mathbf{q}\alpha\ell\beta\ell^{\prime}}\bm{\gamma}_{\mathbf{q}\beta\ell^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\mathbf{D}_{\alpha\beta}^{\ell\ell^{\prime}}(\mathbf{q})\bm{\gamma}_{\mathbf{q}\alpha\ell}, (7)

where 𝐃α​βℓ​ℓ′​(𝐪)\mathbf{D}_{\alpha\beta}^{\ell\ell^{\prime}}(\mathbf{q}) are components of the dynamical matrix and −i​∇𝐑​α​ℓ-i\nabla_{\mathbf{R}\alpha\ell} is conjugate to 𝐮𝐑​α​ℓ\mathbf{u}_{\mathbf{R}\alpha\ell}.

To solve this problem exactly, we proceed to finding the normal modes 𝜸𝐪​α​ℓ\bm{\gamma}_{\mathbf{q}\alpha\ell} that diagonalize 𝐃α​βℓ​ℓ′​(𝐪)\mathbf{D}_{\alpha\beta}^{\ell\ell^{\prime}}(\mathbf{q}) for all 𝐪\mathbf{q} in the mini-Brillouin zone. The associated eigenvalue spectrum λm​(𝐪)\lambda_{m}(\mathbf{q}) with band index m=1,⋯,2​Nm=1,\cdots,2N will then determine the normal mode frequencies as ωm​(𝐪)=λm​(𝐪)\omega_{m}(\mathbf{q})=\sqrt{\lambda_{m}(\mathbf{q})}. Because the dynamical matrix describes the curvature of the Coulomb potential, scaling as 1/rs31/r_{s}^{3}, it follows that ω∝rs−3/2\omega\propto r_{s}^{-3/2} at fixed ts/rst_{s}/r_{s}.

To begin, we consider the simple limit ts/rs→∞t_{s}/r_{s}\to\infty of two decoupled Wigner crystals. In this case, the spectrum contains two degenerate copies of the transverse phonon- and longitudinal plasmon modes characteristic of the monolayer. As ts/rst_{s}/r_{s} is reduced, the interlayer Coulomb interaction lifts the degeneracy and splits them into two pairs of acoustic (in-phase) and optical (out-of-phase motion of the layers) modes. Independently of the twist angle, both the transverse (TA) and longitudinal (LA) acoustic modes remain gapless, due to the translation symmetry of Eq. (1). On the other hand, the twist-angle dependence of uinteru_{\text{inter}} crucially determines the gap of the optical modes via the dispersion relation ω⁡(𝐪,θ)∼ω WC2​(𝐪)+|uinter​(θ)|\omega(\mathbf{q};\theta)\sim\sqrt{\omega_{\scriptscriptstyle\text{ WC}}^{2}(\mathbf{q})+|u_{\text{inter}}(\theta)|}, both transverse (TO) and longitudinal (LO): the 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 gap will range from ∼e−Gts/2\sim e^{-Gt_{s}/2} for the optimally stacked honeycomb bilayer (see Eq. (3)), to an exponentially smaller gap ∼e−G​ts\sim e^{-Gt_{s}} (see Eq. (5)) for the 30∘30^{\circ}-twisted quasicrystal, where interactions between the layers are weakest.

Figure 2 (a)(a)-(c)(c) shows the normal mode spectrum for the honeycomb bilayer (red) and quasicrystal approximant (blue), after folding the honeycomb bands into the same mini-Brillouin zone for direct comparison. The insets provide zoom-ins of the dispersion at small |𝐪||\mathbf{q}|, highlighting the different gap-size, with the monolayer curves (black dashed) serving as a reference.

As anticipated, all four modes remain (almost) gapless in the quasicrystal state. This is a consequence of an emergent non-local continuous relative-shift symmetry: up to exponentially small relaxation effects, shifting one quasicrystal layer relative to the other modifies local patterns but leaves the total energy unchanged, preventing TO and LO modes from developing a gap in a rigid quasicrystal. At small 𝐪\mathbf{q}, the gapless optical modes correspond to a nearly uniform relative displacement of the two layers, with a vanishing energy cost as 𝐪→𝟎\mathbf{q}\to\mathbf{0}. Protected by the relative-shift symmetry, these modes are “phasons” [34]. Unlike regular phonons, the phasons propagate in a diffusive manner, owing to the non-local nature of the shift symmetry [35, 36].

A useful measure of the distribution of collective modes is provided by the density of states DOS​(ω)\text{DOS}(\omega) per particle, which quantifies the number of normal modes in a small frequency range centered around ω\omega. This is shown in Fig. 2 (d)(d) for the case of a honeycomb (red) and large quasicrystal approximant with θ≈29.84∘\theta\approx 29.84^{\circ} (blue). Evidently, the two peaks present in the DOS of decoupled Wigner crystal layers (black dashed) split differently for the two stackings: in the quasicrystal, more weight is carried to lower frequencies and modes up to the first peak closely match the decoupled layers density of states, while in the honeycomb more DOS is shifted to higher energies.

From the density of states, the zero-point energy per particle of a bilayer stacking with twist angle θ\theta can be compactly written as

ZPE​(θ)=12​∫d​ω​ω​DOS​(ω,θ).\displaystyle\text{ZPE}(\theta)=\frac{1}{2}\int\text{d}\omega\ \omega\ \text{DOS}(\omega;\theta). (8)

Fig. 3 (a) gives the zero point energy per particle for different twists angles at ts/rs=3t_{s}/r_{s}=3, defined with respect to the value ZPEWC\rm ZPE_{\rm\scriptscriptstyle WC} for two decoupled layers. As was the case for the the classical energy shown in Fig. 1 (c), the quantum correction has a weaker dependence on the angle θ\theta at larger twists, where the interlayer coupling is small. Crucially, however, the twist angle dependence of the zero-point energy displays the opposite trend: it is minimal for the 30∘30^{\circ}-quasicrystal and grows larger with the twist angle, reaching its maximum with the honeycomb stacking.

With the zero point energy at hand, we are ready to study the total energy ϵ⁡(θ)\epsilon(\theta) of the bilayers as a function of the twist angle, and determine their relative stability – this will ultimately depend on the parameter rsr_{s}, which sets the scale of quantum fluctuations.

We make the rsr_{s} dependence explicit by rewriting u=u~/rsu=\tilde{u}/r_{s} and ZPE=z~/rs3\text{ZPE}=\tilde{z}/r_{s}^{3} where u~​(ts/rs),z~​(ts/rs)\tilde{u}(t_{s}/r_{s}),\tilde{z}(t_{s}/r_{s}) are now functions of the classical parameter ts/rst_{s}/r_{s} only. The total energy per particle at twist angle θ\theta, defined relative to honeycomb stacking, then reads

ϵ⁡(θ)−ϵHC\displaystyle\epsilon(\theta)-\epsilon_{\rm\scriptscriptstyle HC} ≈u~rs+z~rs3/2+O⁡(rs−2),\displaystyle\approx\frac{\tilde{u}}{r_{s}}+\frac{\tilde{z}}{r_{s}^{3/2}}+O(r_{s}^{-2}), (9)

or equivalently, after restoring dimensional factors (aB=4​π​ε​ℏ2/m​e2a_{B}=4\pi\varepsilon\hbar^{2}/me^{2} is the effective Bohr radius),

E⁡(θ)−EHC\displaystyle E(\theta)-E_{\rm HC} ≈e2​(π​n2​D)124​π​ε​[u~+aB​(π​n2​D)12​z~],\displaystyle\approx\frac{e^{2}(\pi n_{\rm 2D})^{\frac{1}{2}}}{4\pi\varepsilon}\left[\tilde{u}+\sqrt{a_{B}(\pi n_{\rm 2D})^{\frac{1}{2}}}\,\tilde{z}\right], (10)

with u~​(ts/rs)>0\tilde{u}(t_{s}/r_{s})>0 and z~​(ts/rs)<0\tilde{z}(t_{s}/r_{s})<0. At very large rsr_{s}, the classical term dominates, and the honeycomb stacking is favored. On the contrary, as rsr_{s} decreases, the zero point energy term dominates Eq. (9) and ϵ⁡(θ)<ϵHC\epsilon(\theta)<\epsilon_{\rm\scriptscriptstyle HC} with the lowest energy associated with the lowest ZPE found at 30∘30^{\circ}.

The first-order phase transition line ϵ⁡(30∘)=ϵHC\epsilon(30^{\circ})=\epsilon_{\rm\scriptscriptstyle HC} is shown in black in Fig. 3(b)\,(b) as a function of rsr_{s} and ts/rst_{s}/r_{s}. The angular dependence of the total energy is displayed in Fig. 3(c)\,(c), and shows that the 30∘30^{\circ}-quasicrystal goes from local- to global minimum upon decreasing rsr_{s}. More details of the phase transition are reported in the supplementary [32]. We have therefore found that the quasicrystal becomes the true ground state when quantum fluctuations are sufficiently large, confirming the genuinely quantum mechanical nature of this state.

Lindemann criterion – The above analysis relies on the harmonic approximation, which becomes invalid as fluctuations increase and eventually melt the crystal stacking into a bilayer Fermi liquid. This calls for an analysis of the Lindemann melting criterion [24, 23], which defines the ordered phase from the condition that average fluctuations cannot exceed a certain fraction of the lattice spacing, i.e.,

γL=maxα⁡⟨|𝐮𝐑​α|2/a2⟩<0.3,\displaystyle\gamma_{\scriptscriptstyle L}=\max_{\alpha}\sqrt{\langle|\mathbf{u}_{\mathbf{R}\alpha}|^{2}/a^{2}\rangle}<0.3, (11)

where the value 0.30.3 is obtained from imposing that the monolayer Wigner crystal melts at rsmono≈31r_{s}^{\rm mono}\approx 31 (correspondingly rs≈22r_{s}\approx 22), as found by QMC on spin-polarized 2D electron gas [37, 38]. This analysis is of particular importance in the case of the 30∘30^{\circ}-quasicrystal, where the weak interlayer coupling and the presence of soft, gapless optical modes conjure to destabilize the crystalline phase.

Figure 4 shows the melting line for the honeycomb and quasicrystal phases as a function of rsr_{s} and tst_{s}. For an honeycomb stacking, zero-point fluctuations become more energetically expensive as the layers are brought closer to another, shifting the melting line [23] to smaller values of rsr_{s} than for decoupled layers (vertical dotted). On the opposite, the quasicrystal stacking saturates the Lindemann criterion already at higher values of rsr_{s}, i.e., for weaker quantum fluctuations. At low ts/rst_{s}/r_{s}, we complete the phase diagram by indicating the classically favored rhombic stacking (orange) and square stacking (green) phases [24] replacing the honeycomb stacking.

Importantly, comparison of Fig. 3(b)\,(b) and Fig. 4 shows that there exists a wide parameter range where the quasicrystal state remains stable and energetically favorable. Finally, we note that the phase diagram in Fig. 4 is in good quantitative agreement with the NN-VMC results reported in Ref. [1].

Discussion – The strongly correlated phases of the homogeneous electron gas constitute the vocabulary of many-body condensed matter physics [39]. In this work, we have analyzed a particular instance of this model – the electron bilayer – and determined its diagram as a function of electron density and layer separation. We identify a broad region of parameter space in which ground state is the electron quasicrystal, and elucidate its quantum mechanical origin. Remarkably, the resulting phase diagram is in excellent agreement with the result of unbiased NN-VMC simulations reported in Ref. [1] for wide quantum wells, confirming the robustness of our conclusions.

The electronic quasicrystal has no classical analogue: it is stabilized by zero-point motion and disappears in the classical limit. This mechanism is generic and suggests that quantum quasicrystals may arise more broadly in systems where competing classical configurations are close in energy, and quantum fluctuations lift the degeneracy.

Since the quantum quasicrystal studied here emerges spontaneously from Coulomb interactions, it is directly accessible in various solid-state platforms, including semiconductor quantum wells, TMD heterostructures and rhombohedral graphene, where signatures of electron crystals have been reported. Its presence could be detected through transport signatures [40], optical probes of excitonic umklapp scattering [11, 10], or direct imaging using scanning tunneling microscopy [12, 13].

Our results connect the rich phenomenology of quasicrystals to the conceptual simplicity of the electron gas, revealing a new surprise in one of the oldest systems in condensed matter physics. Looking ahead, this invites us to think about related novel strongly correlated electronic phases. One intriguing possibility is the formation of a nematic bilayer Fermi liquid with dodecagonal rotational symmetry [41, 42], driven by incommensuration in the vicinity of the quasicrystal melting line. Finally, an interesting direction is the extension of the quantum fluctuation mechanism to bosonic systems, where quantum quasicrystals have been previously proposed for ultracold atom systems with Rashba spin-orbit coupling [43] and engineered long-ranged interactions [44, 45].

I Commensurate Triangular Stackings

To obtain the angle dependence of the classical energy and the normal mode spectrum, we use commensurate bilayer twisted stackings of triangular lattices. Here, we illustrate the details of the construction [47, 48, 49] of the minimal supercell of such stackings.

In layer ℓ\ell, we place a triangular lattice with lattice constant aa, unit cell area A=3​a2/2A=\sqrt{3}a^{2}/2, and primitive vectors 𝐚1ℓ,𝐚2ℓ\mathbf{a}_{1}^{\ell},\mathbf{a}_{2}^{\ell}. The stacking is specified by a rotation by an angle θ\theta of ℓ=2\ell=2 with respect to ℓ=1\ell=1. For a commensurate twist angle θ∈[0,60∘]\theta\in[0,60^{\circ}], the two lattices share special coincidence points forming a superlattice. The associated supercell gives the smallest repeating unit of the bilayer crystal pattern and is generated by primitive vectors 𝐀1,𝐀2\mathbf{A}_{1},\mathbf{A}_{2} that connect neighboring coincidence points.

To construct 𝐀1,𝐀2\mathbf{A}_{1},\mathbf{A}_{2}, we use a complex representation of the monolayer triangular lattices. In layer 11, we choose 𝐚11=1\mathbf{a}_{1}^{1}=1, 𝐚21=ei​π/3\mathbf{a}_{2}^{1}=e^{i\pi/3} such that a general lattice point of this layer is z1=p+q​ei​π/3z_{1}=p+qe^{i\pi/3} for integers p,qp,q. In parallel, points z2z_{2} of layer 22 are obtained by θ\theta rotation as z2=z1​ei​θz_{2}=z_{1}e^{i\theta}. It follows that the coincidence condition z1′=z2z_{1}^{\prime}=z_{2} for the two layers can be recast in terms of points of layer 11 as ei​θ=z1/z1′e^{i\theta}=z_{1}/z_{1}^{\prime}.

Given that θ\theta is a commensurate twist, a solution with minimal length |z1|=|z1′||z_{1}|=|z_{1}^{\prime}| is provided by the unique factorization property of the Eisenstein integers [47] as z1=Zz_{1}=Z and z1′=Z⋆z_{1}^{\prime}=Z^{\star} where Z=p+q​ei​π/3Z=p+qe^{i\pi/3} for the coprime integers (p,q)(p,q) and p≠q​mod​ 3p\neq q\ \text{mod}\ 3 [48]. We have therefore found that, at commensurate twist angle θ\theta, the first superlattice primitive vector is given by

cos⁡(θ)=Re​(ZZ⋆)=p2+p​q−q2/2p2+p​q+q2.\displaystyle\cos(\theta)=\text{Re}\left(\frac{Z}{Z^{\star}}\right)=\frac{p^{2}+pq-q^{2}/2}{p^{2}+pq+q^{2}}. (1)

To find a pair of them, we simply have to use that rotations of both layers by ei​π/3e^{i\pi/3} leave the full stacking unchanged, which yields that Z​ei​π/3Ze^{i\pi/3} is also a superlattice point (with the same minimal length as ZZ). The supercell primitive vectors therefore reads

𝐀1=Z=p​𝐚11+q​𝐚21,𝐀2=ei​π/3​Z=−q​𝐚11+(p+q)​𝐚21.\displaystyle\mathbf{A}_{1}=Z=p\mathbf{a}_{1}^{1}+q\mathbf{a}_{2}^{1},\quad\mathbf{A}_{2}=e^{i\pi/3}Z=-q\mathbf{a}_{1}^{1}+(p+q)\mathbf{a}_{2}^{1}. (2)

The basis pattern of the supercell spanned by 𝐀1,2\mathbf{A}_{1,2} is specified by NN points where

N=2​As.c.A=2​(p2+p​q+q2)\displaystyle N=2\frac{A_{\rm s.c.}}{A}=2(p^{2}+pq+q^{2}) (3)

and density is n2​D=N/As.c.n_{\rm 2D}=N/A_{\rm s.c.}. Incommensurate angles such as 30∘30^{\circ} are N→∞N\to\infty limits of a (p,q)(p,q) sequence of approximants. The first five angles and associated (p,q)(p,q) pairs in the 30∘30^{\circ} approximant sequence are listed in Table 1.

In reciprocal space, the superlattice generated by 𝐀1,𝐀2\mathbf{A}_{1},\mathbf{A}_{2} has primitive vectors

𝐁1=2​πAs.c.z^×𝐀2,𝐁2=−2​πAs.c.z^×𝐀1\displaystyle\mathbf{B}_{1}=\frac{2\pi}{A_{\rm s.c.}}\hat{z}\times\mathbf{A}_{2},\quad\mathbf{B}_{2}=-\frac{2\pi}{A_{\rm s.c.}}\hat{z}\times\mathbf{A}_{1}

In a crystal with the periodicity of the superlattice, the phonon modes have wave vectors 𝐪\mathbf{q} within the mini-Brillouin zone of this reciprocal lattice.

An interesting dual problem relevant to the analysis of Section III consists in finding the coincidence points of the twisted reciprocal lattices of each layer. The reciprocal lattice associated with layer ℓ\ell has primitive vectors

𝐛1ℓ=2​πAz^×𝐚2ℓ,𝐛2ℓ=−2​πAz^×𝐚1ℓ\displaystyle\mathbf{b}_{1}^{\ell}=\frac{2\pi}{A}\hat{z}\times\mathbf{a}_{2}^{\ell},\quad\mathbf{b}_{2}^{\ell}=-\frac{2\pi}{A}\hat{z}\times\mathbf{a}_{1}^{\ell} (4)

with norm G=4​π/3​aG=4\pi/\sqrt{3}a. Adapting the above results, the coincidence points of reciprocal lattices 1,21,2 form a super- reciprocal lattice generated by primitive vectors 𝐁1r\mathbf{B}_{1}^{\rm r}, 𝐁2r\mathbf{B}_{2}^{\rm r}. When layer 11 and 22 are twisted by an angle θ\theta, the reciprocal lattices are also twisted by θ\theta corresponding to the same pair of integers (p,q)(p,q) as the direct lattice. It follows that |𝐁1r|2=|𝐁2r|2=G2​(p2+p​q+q2)=G2​N/2|\mathbf{B}_{1}^{\rm r}|^{2}=|\mathbf{B}_{2}^{\rm r}|^{2}=G^{2}(p^{2}+pq+q^{2})=G^{2}N/2 are inversely proportional to |𝐁1|2=|𝐁2|2=2​G2/N|\mathbf{B}_{1}|^{2}=|\mathbf{B}_{2}|^{2}=2G^{2}/N.

II Ewald Summation

For a sequence of commensurate angles with N≤402N\leq 402, we relax the rigid triangular stacking supercells in periodic boundary conditions following the gradient of the Coulomb potential. The equilibrium configuration of electron α\alpha in layer ℓ\ell is specified by 𝐫α,ℓ=(𝝆α,ℓ,zα,ℓ)\mathbf{r}_{\alpha,\ell}=(\bm{\rho}_{\alpha,\ell},z_{\alpha,\ell}) and the associated value of the potential per unit cell is reported in Fig. 1 (c). In a commensurate stacking with Ns.cellN_{\rm s.cell} copies of the supercell in periodic boundary conditions, we consider small displacements from equilibrium of the form given by Eq. (6): plane waves over the superlattice sites 𝐑\mathbf{R} with wave vector 𝐪\mathbf{q} in the mini-Brillouin zone of the superlattice, modulated by an internal displacement pattern 𝜸α​ℓ​𝐪\bm{\gamma}_{\alpha\ell\mathbf{q}} that repeats from one supercell to the next. The residual superlattice translation symmetry decouples modes in distinct 𝐪\mathbf{q} sectors, so the normal-mode spectrum shown in Fig. 2(a) is obtained by diagonalizing the 2​N×2​N2N\times 2N dynamical matrix at each 𝐪\mathbf{q}.

Both the classical equilibrium configuration and the dynamical matrix require lattice sums of the long-range Coulomb interaction, which we evaluate using Ewald summation. In this section, we give the Ewald summation for the Coulomb potential and dynamical matrix elements. The rely on

S⁡(𝐪,𝐫)=∑′𝐑′​ei​𝐪⋅𝐑|𝐑+𝐫|\displaystyle S(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{r})=\sideset{}{{}^{\prime}}{\sum}_{\mathbf{R}}\frac{e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}}}{\left|\mathbf{R}+\mathbf{r}\right|} (5)

where 𝐑\mathbf{R} ranges over superlattice sites and 𝐫=(𝝆,z)\mathbf{r}=(\bm{\rho},z). The prime sum ∑′\sum^{{}^{\prime}} indicates we exclude 𝐑=𝟎\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{0} when 𝐫=𝟎\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{0}. Following [33, 24], we split S⁡(𝐪,𝐫)S(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{r}) into direct and reciprocal components S=Sdir.+Srec.S=S_{\rm dir.}+S_{\rm rec.}:

Sdir.(𝐪,𝐫)=1π∑′𝐑′ei​𝐪⋅𝐑∫γ∞t−1/2e−t​z2e−t​|𝐑+𝝆|2dt,\displaystyle S_{\rm dir.}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}}\sideset{}{{}^{\prime}}{\sum}_{\mathbf{R}}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}}\int_{\gamma}^{\infty}t^{-1/2}e^{-tz^{2}}e^{-t|\mathbf{R}+\bm{\rho}|^{2}}\,dt, (6)
Srec.(𝐪,𝐫)=1π∑𝐑ei​𝐪⋅𝐑∫0γt−1/2e−t​z2e−t​|𝐑+𝝆|2dt−δ𝐫,𝟎1π∫0γt−1/2dt.\displaystyle S_{\rm rec.}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}}\sum_{\mathbf{R}}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}}\int_{0}^{\gamma}t^{-1/2}e^{-tz^{2}}e^{-t|\mathbf{R}+\bm{\rho}|^{2}}\,dt-\delta_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{0}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}}\int_{0}^{\gamma}t^{-1/2}\,dt. (7)

The splitting is controlled by γ\gamma and we used the efficient value γ=(2.4/As.c)2\gamma=(2.4/\sqrt{A_{\rm s.c}})^{2} [50]. −2​πAs.c.​(z​erf​(γ1/2​z)+1π​γ​e−γ​z2)​δ𝐪,𝟎−2​γπ​δ𝐫,𝟎\displaystyle\hskip 56.9055pt-\frac{2\pi}{A_{\rm s.c.}}\left(z\text{erf}(\gamma^{1/2}z)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi\gamma}}e^{-\gamma z^{2}}\right)\delta_{\mathbf{q},\mathbf{0}}-\frac{2\sqrt{\gamma}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\delta_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{0}} (9)

The elements of the dynamical matrix [51] are given by

(13)

III General Scalings

The mechanism underlying the angle dependence of our results is illustrated by examining the interlayer Coulomb interaction energy per particle uinteru_{\rm inter} for a basis 𝐫α,ℓ=(𝝆α,ℓ,zα,ℓ)\mathbf{r}_{\alpha,\ell}=(\bm{\rho}_{\alpha,\ell},z_{\alpha,\ell}). In momentum space, this energy can be written as

uinter\displaystyle u_{\rm inter} =12​N​∑α​β,ℓ≠ℓ′∑𝐑1|𝐑+𝐫α​ℓ−𝐫β​ℓ′|+n2​D​π​ts2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{\alpha\beta,\ell\neq\ell^{\prime}}\sum_{\mathbf{R}}\ \frac{1}{|\mathbf{R}+\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\ell}-\mathbf{r}_{\beta\ell^{\prime}}|}+\frac{n_{\rm 2D}\pi t_{s}}{2}
=12​N​∑α​β,ℓ≠ℓ′(−2​πAs.c.​ts+2​πAs.c.​∑𝐆≠𝟎e−|𝐆|​ts|𝐆|​ei​𝐆⋅(𝐫α,ℓ−𝐫β,ℓ′))+n2​D​π​ts2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{\alpha\beta,\ell\neq\ell^{\prime}}\left(-\frac{2\pi}{A_{\rm s.c.}}t_{s}+\frac{2\pi}{A_{\rm s.c.}}\sum_{\mathbf{G}\neq\mathbf{0}}\frac{e^{-|\mathbf{G}|t_{s}}}{|\mathbf{G}|}e^{i\mathbf{G}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_{\alpha,\ell}-\mathbf{r}_{\beta,\ell^{\prime}})}\right)+\frac{n_{\rm 2D}\pi t_{s}}{2}
=π​n2​D2​∑𝐆≠𝟎e−|𝐆|​ts|𝐆|​Re​[ρ1​(𝐆)​ρ2​(−𝐆)]\displaystyle=\frac{\pi n_{\rm 2D}}{2}\sum_{\mathbf{G}\neq\mathbf{0}}\frac{e^{-|\mathbf{G}|t_{s}}}{|\mathbf{G}|}\mathrm{Re}[\rho_{1}(\mathbf{G})\rho_{2}(-\mathbf{G})] (14)

where 𝐆\mathbf{G} ranges over the reciprocal lattice of the superlattice and ρℓ​(𝐆)=2N​∑αei​𝐆⋅𝐫α,ℓ\rho_{\ell}(\mathbf{G})=\frac{2}{N}\sum_{\alpha}e^{i\mathbf{G}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{\alpha,\ell}}. The interlayer interaction is controlled by the weight Re⁡[ρ1​(𝐆)​ρ2​(−𝐆)]\mathrm{Re}[\rho_{1}(\mathbf{G})\rho_{2}(-\mathbf{G})] that selects the contributing 𝐆\mathbf{G}. For a honeycomb stacking, the relative shift 𝐬\mathbf{s} in the origin of the two layers gives Re⁡[ρ1​(𝐆)​ρ2​(−𝐆)]=cos⁡(𝐆⋅𝐬)<0\mathrm{Re}[\rho_{1}(\mathbf{G})\rho_{2}(-\mathbf{G})]=\cos(\mathbf{G} \cdot\mathbf{s})<0 and 𝐆\mathbf{G} runs over the monolayer reciprocal lattice shared by layers 11 and 22. This negative contribution reflects the tendency of layers to relax towards A​BAB stacking to lower their energy relative to the decoupled limit.

We now contrast the behavior of the unrelaxed ρℓU\rho^{U}_{\ell} and relaxed ρℓR\rho^{R}_{\ell} density Fourier components for twisted configuration. For a general commensurate twist without relaxation, 𝐫α​ℓ=𝐫α​ℓU\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\ell}=\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\ell}^{U} is a rigid triangular lattice in each layer. The resulting Re​[ρ1U​(𝐆)​ρ2U​(−𝐆)]\text{Re}[\rho_{1}^{U}(\mathbf{G})\rho_{2}^{U}(-\mathbf{G})] only has peaks at coincidence points of the triangular reciprocal lattices of layers 11 and 22, which form the super- reciprocal lattice discussed at the end of Sec. I. Before relaxation, the shortest non-zero coinciding reciprocal vectors for generic twist have modulus |𝐆|2=G2​N/2|\mathbf{G}|^{2}=G^{2}N/2 and their contribution are exponentially suppressed with exp⁡(−G​ts​N/2)\exp(- G t_s\sqrt{N/2} ), making them negligible.

In the relaxed case, 𝐫α​ℓR=𝐫α​ℓU+δ​𝐫ℓ​(𝐫α​ℓU)\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\ell}^{R}=\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\ell}^{U}+\delta\mathbf{r}_{\ell}(\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\ell}^{U}) where δ​𝐫ℓ\delta\mathbf{r}_{\ell} is the displacement at 𝐫α​ℓU\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\ell}^{U} caused by relaxation of layer ℓ\ell. This displacement repeats with the periodicity of the superlattice and can therefore be expanded in associated Fourier mode 𝐠\mathbf{g} as δ​𝐫ℓ​(𝐫)=∑𝐠𝒂ℓ,𝐠​ei​𝐠⋅𝝆\delta\mathbf{r}_{\ell}(\mathbf{r})=\sum_{\mathbf{g}}\bm{a}_{\ell,\mathbf{g}}e^{i\mathbf{g}\cdot\bm{\rho}}. We take 𝐚ℓ,𝟎=𝟎\mathbf{a}_{\ell,\mathbf{0}}=\mathbf{0} by absorbing uniform relative shifts of the layers into the unrelaxed configuration. For small δ​𝐫ℓ\delta\mathbf{r}_{\ell}, it follows that the Fourier components of the relaxed density are

ρℓR​(𝐆)\displaystyle\rho_{\ell}^{R}(\mathbf{G}) =∑αei​𝐆⋅𝐫α​ℓU​(1+i​𝐆⋅δ​𝐫ℓ​(𝐫α​ℓU))+O⁡(δ​𝐫ℓ2)=ρℓU​(𝐆)+i​𝐆⋅∑𝐠ρℓU​(𝐆+𝐠)​𝐚ℓ,𝐠+O⁡(δ​𝐫ℓ2).\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha}e^{i\mathbf{G}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\ell}^{U}}(1+i\mathbf{G}\cdot\delta\mathbf{r}_{\ell}(\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\ell}^{U}))+O(\delta\mathbf{r}^{2}_{\ell})=\rho_{\ell}^{U}(\mathbf{G})+i\mathbf{G}\cdot\sum_{\mathbf{g}}\rho_{\ell}^{U}(\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{g})\mathbf{a}_{\ell,\mathbf{g}}+O(\delta\mathbf{r}^{2}_{\ell}). (15)

Compared to ρℓU\rho_{\ell}^{U}, the relaxed Fourier components ρℓR\rho_{\ell}^{R} feature a richer set of peaks: layer ℓ\ell acquires contributions from reciprocal vectors 𝐆\mathbf{G} of layer ℓ′\ell^{\prime}, provided 𝐠+𝐆\mathbf{g}+\mathbf{G} still belongs to the reciprocal lattice of layer ℓ\ell. In particular, we can simultaneously have 𝐆\mathbf{G} in the reciprocal lattice of layer 22, so that ρ2R​(−𝐆)≠0\rho_{2}^{R}(-\mathbf{G})\neq 0, and 𝐠+𝐆\mathbf{g}+\mathbf{G} in that of layer 11, so that ρ1R​(𝐆+𝐠)≠0\rho_{1}^{R}(\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{g})\neq 0.

To first order in δ​𝐫ℓ\delta\mathbf{r}_{\ell}, the interlayer interaction for the component 𝐆\mathbf{G} is then proportional to

Re​[ρ1R​(𝐆)​ρ2R​(−𝐆)]\displaystyle\text{Re}[\rho_{1}^{R}(\mathbf{G})\rho_{2}^{R}(-\mathbf{G})] =Re​[ρ1U​(𝐆)​ρ2U​(−𝐆)]\displaystyle=\text{Re}[\rho_{1}^{U}(\mathbf{G})\rho_{2}^{U}(-\mathbf{G})]
+Re​[i​𝐆⋅∑𝐠(ρ1U​(𝐆+𝐠)​ρ2U​(−𝐆)​𝐚1,𝐠−ρ1U​(𝐆)​ρ2U​(−𝐆+𝐠)​𝐚2,𝐠)]+O⁡(δ​𝐫ℓ2)\displaystyle\quad\quad+\text{Re}\left[i\mathbf{G}\cdot\sum_{\mathbf{g}}\left(\rho_{1}^{U}(\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{g})\rho_{2}^{U}(-\mathbf{G})\mathbf{a}_{1,\mathbf{g}}-\rho_{1}^{U}(\mathbf{G})\rho_{2}^{U}(-\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{g})\mathbf{a}_{2,\mathbf{g}}\right)\right]+O(\delta\mathbf{r}_{\ell}^{2}) (16)

The cross terms in Eq. 16 typically dominate over the negligible unrelaxed contribution Re​[ρ1U​(𝐆)​ρ2U​(−𝐆)]\text{Re}[\rho_{1}^{U}(\mathbf{G})\rho_{2}^{U}(-\mathbf{G})], and are maximal for relaxation wavevectors 𝐠=𝐆1−𝐆2\mathbf{g}=\mathbf{G}_{1}-\mathbf{G}_{2} with |𝐠|=2​G​sin⁡(θ/2)∼LM−1|\mathbf{g}|=2G\sin(\theta/2)\sim L_{M}^{-1} setting the inverse moiré length scale. In Fig. 1 (c-f), we show an example of the effect of relaxation on the contribution of 𝐆ℓ\mathbf{G}_{\ell} to Re​[ρ1​(𝐆)​ρ2​(−𝐆)]\text{Re}[\rho_{1}(\mathbf{G})\rho_{2}(-\mathbf{G})]. As expected, unrelaxed Re​[ρ1U​(𝐆)​ρ2U​(−𝐆)]\text{Re}[\rho_{1}^{U}(\mathbf{G})\rho_{2}^{U}(-\mathbf{G})] (e) does not feature peaks at small non-zero 𝐆ℓ\mathbf{G}_{\ell} and (f) shows how these peaks are developed through relaxation.

While Re​[ρ1R​(𝐆)​ρ2R​(−𝐆)]≠0\text{Re}[\rho_{1}^{R}(\mathbf{G})\rho_{2}^{R}(-\mathbf{G})]\neq 0 is realized in principle for every 𝐆ℓ\mathbf{G}_{\ell}, exponential suppression e−|𝐆|​tse^{-|\mathbf{G}|t_{s}} selects the minimal non-zero |𝐆|=G|\mathbf{G}|=G shell as the dominant contribution. Another essential factor influencing the contribution of 𝐆ℓ\mathbf{G}_{\ell} is the Fourier component 𝐚ℓ,𝐠\mathbf{a}_{\ell,\mathbf{g}}. In what follows, we obtain the scaling of 𝐚ℓ,𝐠\mathbf{a}_{\ell,\mathbf{g}} with well thickness and its angle dependence which carries over to our general results for classical and zero point energy.

We argued in the main text that, for sufficiently large ts/rst_{s}/r_{s} at a finite twist, relaxation contributes in a perturbative way. In this regime, we found δ​𝐫∼e−G​ts​LM2/a\delta\mathbf{r}\sim e^{-Gt_{s}}L_{M}^{2}/a and we now provide a more precise version of this result. We focus the displacement δ​𝐫1\delta\mathbf{r}_{1} induced by relaxation.

We start by expanding δ​𝐫1\delta\mathbf{r}_{1} against the normal modes of a triangular Wigner crystal in layer 11:

δ​𝐫1​(𝐫)=∑𝐪(a1,𝐪T​𝐞1,𝐪T+a1,𝐪L​𝐞1,𝐪L)​ei​𝐪⋅𝝆\displaystyle\delta\mathbf{r}_{1}(\mathbf{r})=\sum_{\mathbf{q}}(a_{1,\mathbf{q}}^{T}\mathbf{e}^{T}_{1,\mathbf{q}}+a_{1,\mathbf{q}}^{L}\mathbf{e}^{L}_{1,\mathbf{q}})e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\bm{\rho}} (17)

where ωT​(𝐪)\omega_{T}(\mathbf{q}) and ωL​(𝐪)\omega_{L}(\mathbf{q}) are the acoustic phonon and longitudinal plasmon frequencies with respective polarizations 𝐞T=z^×q^\mathbf{e}^{T}=\hat{z}\times\hat{q} and 𝐞L=q^\mathbf{e}^{L}=\hat{q}. Here 𝐪\mathbf{q} belongs to the Brillouin zone of monolayer Wigner crystal. However, as stated above, we suppose that relaxation repeats with the periodicity of the superlattice and only specific 𝐪=𝐠\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{g} in the reciprocal superlattice are allowed. With this in mind, we write the forces acting on the electron with an unrelaxed position 𝐫\mathbf{r} with displacement δ​𝐫1\delta\mathbf{r}_{1}. The elastic intra-layer restoring force is

𝐅intra(𝐫)=−∑𝐪(ωT(𝐪)2a1,𝐪T𝐞1,𝐪T+ωL(𝐪)2a1,𝐪L𝐞1,𝐪L)ei​𝐪⋅𝝆.\displaystyle\mathbf{F}_{\rm intra}(\mathbf{r})=-\sum_{\mathbf{q}}(\omega_{T}(\mathbf{q})^{2}a_{1,\mathbf{q}}^{T}\mathbf{e}^{T}_{1,\mathbf{q}}+\omega_{L}(\mathbf{q})^{2}a_{1,\mathbf{q}}^{L}\mathbf{e}^{L}_{1,\mathbf{q}})e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\bm{\rho}}. (18)

The force applied by layer 22 depends on the relaxation of this layer. However, the dominant contribution to this force is captured by the potential sourced by the unrelaxed configuration of layer 22, which only has Fourier components at reciprocal lattice vectors 𝐆2\mathbf{G}_{2} of the rigid triangular layer 22. Neglecting exponentially supressed shells with |𝐆2|>G|\mathbf{G}_{2}|>G, the force associated with the rigid configuration is

𝐅inter​(𝐫)\displaystyle\mathbf{F}_{\rm inter}(\mathbf{r}) =−iπn2​D∑|𝐆2|=G𝐆2Gei​𝐆2⋅𝝆e−G​ts\displaystyle=-i\pi n_{\rm 2D}\sum_{|\mathbf{G}_{2}|=G}\frac{\mathbf{G}_{2}}{G}e^{i\mathbf{G}_{2}\cdot\bm{\rho}}e^{-Gt_{s}} (19)

To make contact with the intra layer force, we express 𝐅inter\mathbf{F}_{\rm inter} in the basis of plane waves on layer 11 by translating 𝐆2\mathbf{G}_{2} vectors back to the Brillouin zone of layer 11. For the shell with |𝐆2|=G|\mathbf{G}_{2}|=G, this process yields components at 𝐠\mathbf{g} moiré vectors with |𝐠|=2​G​sin⁡(θ/2)|\mathbf{g}|=2G\sin(\theta/2) since ei​𝐆2⋅𝝆=ei⁡(𝐠+𝐆1)⋅𝝆=ei​𝐠⋅𝝆e^{i\mathbf{G}_{2}\cdot\bm{\rho}}=e^{i(\mathbf{g}+\mathbf{G}_{1})\cdot\bm{\rho}}=e^{i\mathbf{g}\cdot\bm{\rho}} for 𝐫\mathbf{r} in the rigid triangular lattice of layer 11. The path of folded 𝐆2\mathbf{G}_{2} as a function of θ\theta is given Fig. S2 (a). We have

𝐅inter(𝐫)=−iπn2​D∑|𝐠|=2​G​sin⁡(θ/2)1Gei​𝐠⋅𝝆e−G​ts((𝐆2⋅𝐞𝐠T)𝐞𝐠T+(𝐆2⋅𝐞𝐠L)𝐞𝐠L).\displaystyle\mathbf{F}_{\rm inter}(\mathbf{r})=-i\pi n_{\rm 2D}\sum_{|\mathbf{g}|=2G\sin(\theta/2)}\frac{1}{G}e^{i\mathbf{g}\cdot\bm{\rho}}e^{-Gt_{s}}((\mathbf{G}_{2}\cdot\mathbf{e}^{T}_{\mathbf{g}})\mathbf{e}^{T}_{\mathbf{g}}+(\mathbf{G}_{2}\cdot\mathbf{e}^{L}_{\mathbf{g}})\mathbf{e}^{L}_{\mathbf{g}}).

Balancing the forces, Fourier component by Fourier component, we have

a1,𝐠T=i​π​n2​DωT​(𝐠)2​e−G​ts​cos⁡(θ/2)anda1,𝐠L=−i​π​n2​DωL​(𝐠)2​e−G​ts​sin⁡(θ/2)\displaystyle a_{1,\mathbf{g}}^{T}=\frac{i\pi n_{\rm 2D}}{\omega_{T}(\mathbf{g})^{2}}e^{-Gt_{s}}\cos(\theta/2)\quad\text{and}\quad a_{1,\mathbf{g}}^{L}=-\frac{i\pi n_{\rm 2D}}{\omega_{L}(\mathbf{g})^{2}}e^{-Gt_{s}}\sin(\theta/2) (20)

indicating that the effect of relaxation is set by frequencies of the T,LT,L modes evaluated (see Fig. S2 (b)) over the folded 𝐆2\mathbf{G}_{2} path of Fig. S2 (a). For angles approaching 30∘30^{\circ}, 𝐠\mathbf{g} move towards the Brillouin zone boundary. There, Fig. S2 (b) shows that the 𝐠\mathbf{g} dependence of frequencies saturates to satisfy ∂ω/∂q⟂=0\partial\omega/\partial q_{\perp}=0 at the boundary. It follows that maximal frequencies and minimal relaxation occur at 30∘30^{\circ} with a weaker angle dependence close to 30∘30^{\circ}.

Looking at the denominators of Eq. 20, we observe that the dominant components a1,𝐠a_{1,\mathbf{g}} are associated with minimal transverse mode frequencies ωT≈cT​|𝐪|\omega_{T}\approx c_{T}|\mathbf{q}| where cTc_{T} is the speed of sound. The corresponding displacement is

δ​𝐫1​(𝐫)≈i​∑|𝐠|=2​G​sin⁡(θ/2)π​n2​DcT2​|𝐠|2​e−G​ts​cos⁡(θ/2)​ei​𝐠⋅𝝆​z^×g^∼LM2a​e−G​ts.\displaystyle\delta\mathbf{r}_{1}(\mathbf{r})\approx i\sum_{|\mathbf{g}|=2G\sin(\theta/2)}\frac{\pi n_{\rm 2D}}{c_{T}^{2}|\mathbf{g}|^{2}}e^{-Gt_{s}}\cos(\theta/2)e^{i\mathbf{g}\cdot\bm{\rho}}\hat{z}\times\hat{g}\sim\frac{L_{M}^{2}}{a}e^{-Gt_{s}}. (21)

Carrying the same analysis and approximations for layer 22, we find δ​𝐫2​(𝐫)=−δ​𝐫1​(𝐫)\delta\mathbf{r}_{2}(\mathbf{r})=-\delta\mathbf{r}_{1}(\mathbf{r}). The general small angle scaling of Eq.(21) is verified numerically in Fig. S1 (b) and is consistent with the analogous results in the context of twisted bilayer graphene [29, 30].

With the displacement induced by relaxation, we can find the equillirbium Coulomb energy per particle by substitution into Eq. 14 and into the elastic expansion of intralayer energy per particle

uintra=uWC+14​∑ℓ∑𝐠(ωT​(q)2​|aℓ,𝐠T|2+ωL​(q)2​|aℓ,𝐠L|2)\displaystyle u_{\rm intra}=u_{\rm\scriptscriptstyle WC}+\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\ell}\sum_{\mathbf{g}}(\omega_{T}(q)^{2}|a_{\ell,\mathbf{g}}^{T}|^{2}+\omega_{L}(q)^{2}|a_{\ell,\mathbf{g}}^{L}|^{2})

From Eq. 16, the exponentially supressed interlayer interaction combines with the exponential supression of relaxation induced Bragg peaks ∝𝐚ℓ,𝐠\propto\mathbf{a}_{\ell,\mathbf{g}} to yield uinter∼LM2​e−2​G​ts/au_{\rm inter}\sim L_{M}^{2}e^{-2Gt_{s}}/a. The intralayer interaction relative to uWCu_{\rm\scriptscriptstyle WC} contributes at O⁡(δ​𝐫ℓ2)O(\delta\mathbf{r}_{\ell}^{2}) with the same scaling uintra∼ω​(𝐠)2​δ​𝐫ℓ2∼LM2​e−2​G​ts/au_{\rm intra}\sim\omega(\mathbf{g})^{2}\delta\mathbf{r}^{2}_{\ell}\sim L_{M}^{2}e^{-2Gt_{s}}/a. It follows that u−uWCu-u_{\rm\scriptscriptstyle WC} globally features this shared scaling. We verify this claim in Fig. S1 (a). We compare with honeycomb stacking for which there is no relaxation and where the rigid interlayer interaction directly sets u∼e−G​ts/au\sim e^{-Gt_{s}}/a.

IV Soft modes

In the limit of fully decoupled layers, the phonon spectrum consists of two copies of the monolayer Wigner crystal spectrum. Each layer ℓ\ell supports a transverse acoustic mode of frequency ωℓ​T​(𝐪)\omega_{\ell T}(\mathbf{q}) and a longitudinal plasmon mode of frequency ωℓ​L​(𝐪)\omega_{\ell L}(\mathbf{q}), defined within its own Brillouin zone.

As ts/rst_{s}/r_{s} is reduced, the interlayer interaction grows and couples phonons from the two layers. This coupling breaks the independent translation symmetry of each layer down to the periodicity of the commensurate supercell, and the natural object in reciprocal space becomes the mini-Brillouin zone (mBZ) of the superlattice, constructed from 𝐁1\mathbf{B}_{1} and 𝐁2\mathbf{B}_{2} (see Section I). Different 𝐪\mathbf{q} sectors of the mBZ remain decoupled, and within each sector the leading effect of the interlayer interaction is to lift the degeneracy between modes of nearly identical frequency.

In aligned stackings such as honeycomb, modes from the two layers are degenerate at every 𝐪\mathbf{q}, and the interlayer coupling lifts this degeneracy throughout the mBZ. At finite twist, the same mBZ wavevector probes different symmetry directions from the Brillouin of each layer, so the modes are already non-degenerate at the decoupled level – except in the long-wavelength limit, where isotropy restores ω1​m​(𝐪)=ω2​m​(𝐪)≡ωm​(𝐪)\omega_{1m}(\mathbf{q})=\omega_{2m}(\mathbf{q})\equiv\omega_{m}(\mathbf{q}), with ωT=cT​|𝐪|\omega_{T}=c_{T}|\mathbf{q}| and ωL=π​n2​D​|𝐪|\omega_{L}=\sqrt{\pi n_{\rm 2D}|\mathbf{q}|} (cTc_{T} the transverse speed of sound). The mismatch is maximal at large wavelengths for 30∘30^{\circ}, where the two Brillouin zones are maximally rotated relative to one another and the dispersion minima of one layer fall on maxima of the other. The mixing of the two modes is weak, and only the small isotropic region near 𝐪=𝟎\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{0} feels the effect of interlayer coupling strongly.

We now compute the degeneracy lifting for the soft transverse and longitudinal modes near 𝐪=𝟎\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{0}, where the two layers contribute degenerate copies and the interlayer interaction acts most strongly. The honeycomb and quasicrystal stackings are compared in Fig. 2(b,c)\,(b,c). The relevant normal modes carry a wavevector 𝐪\mathbf{q} that lies simultaneously within the Brillouin zone of each individual layer and within the mBZ of the supercell. In the Brillouin zone of layer ℓ\ell, mode m=T,Lm=T,L takes the form 𝐞m​(𝐪)​ei​𝐪⋅𝐑\mathbf{e}_{m}(\mathbf{q})\,e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}}, where 𝐞m\mathbf{e}_{m} is the polarization of the single electron in the monolayer basis and 𝐑\mathbf{R} runs over monolayer sites. To make contact with modes of the other layer, we re-express this mode in the mBZ as 𝐞m,α,ℓ​(𝐪)​ei​𝐪⋅𝐑′\mathbf{e}_{m,\alpha,\ell}(\mathbf{q})\,e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}^{\prime}} with

𝐞m,α,ℓ(𝐪)=(N/2)−1/2𝐞m(𝐪)ei​𝐪⋅𝐫α,ℓ,\displaystyle\mathbf{e}_{m,\alpha,\ell}(\mathbf{q})=(N/2)^{-1/2}\,\mathbf{e}_{m}(\mathbf{q})\,e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{\alpha,\ell}}, (22)

and 𝐑′\mathbf{R}^{\prime} now runs over superlattice vectors. Projecting the dynamical matrix onto these four modes – two polarizations m=T,Lm=T,L for each of the two layers ℓ=1,2\ell=1,2 – yields a 4×44\times 4 matrix with components

Dm​m′ℓ​ℓ′​(𝐪)\displaystyle D^{\ell\ell^{\prime}}_{mm^{\prime}}(\mathbf{q}) =∑α​β(𝐞m′,β,ℓ′)†​𝐃α​βℓ​ℓ′​(𝐪)​𝐞m,α,ℓ\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\beta}\left(\mathbf{e}_{m^{\prime},\beta,\ell^{\prime}}\right)^{\dagger}\mathbf{D}^{\ell\ell^{\prime}}_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{q})\,\mathbf{e}_{m,\alpha,\ell}
=∑α​β,μ​ν(−∂μ∂νS(𝐪,𝐫α​ℓ−𝐫β​ℓ′)+δα​βδℓ​ℓ′∑β′​ℓ′′∂μ∂νS(𝟎,𝐫α​ℓ−𝐫β′​ℓ′′))(em′,β,ℓ′ν)⋆em,α,ℓμ,\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\beta,\mu\nu}\bigg(-\partial_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}S(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\ell}-\mathbf{r}_{\beta\ell^{\prime}})+\delta_{\alpha\beta}\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\sum_{\beta^{\prime}\ell^{\prime\prime}}\partial_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}S(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{r}_{\alpha\ell}-\mathbf{r}_{\beta^{\prime}\ell^{\prime\prime}})\bigg)(e^{\nu}_{m^{\prime},\beta,\ell^{\prime}})^{\star}\,e^{\mu}_{m,\alpha,\ell}, (23)

where,

∂μ∂νS(𝐪,𝐫)=−2​πAs.c.∑𝐆≠𝐪(𝐆−𝐪)μ(𝐆−𝐪)νei⁡(𝐆−𝐪)⋅𝝆|𝐆−𝐪|e−|𝐆−𝐪|​|z|.\displaystyle\partial_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}S(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{r})=-\frac{2\pi}{A_{\rm s.c.}}\sum_{\mathbf{G}\neq\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{q})_{\mu}(\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{q})_{\nu}\,\frac{e^{i(\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{q})\cdot\bm{\rho}}}{|\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{q}|}\,e^{-|\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{q}||z|}. (24)

While the LL and TT sectors are exactly decoupled at 𝐪=𝟎\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{0} by C3C_{3} symmetry, away from Γ\Gamma the longitudinal plasmon ωL∼|𝐪|1/2\omega_{L}\sim|\mathbf{q}|^{1/2} and the transverse mode ωT∼|𝐪|\omega_{T}\sim|\mathbf{q}| are split by a frequency ratio ωL/ωT→∞\omega_{L}/\omega_{T}\to\infty as 𝐪→𝟎\mathbf{q}\to\mathbf{0}, suppressing LL–TT mixing at small |𝐪||\mathbf{q}|. The 4×44\times 4 matrix therefore reduces to two independent 2×22\times 2 blocks, one per polarization. Their components are

with

Of particular interest, the ΩL−​(𝐪)\Omega_{L}^{-}(\mathbf{q}) LO phason mode consists of out of phase longitudinal excitations in each layer. An over-density of one layer is paired with an under-density of the other, making the excitation neutral in plane with behavior governed by dipole-dipole interaction. For the quasicrystal, neglecting the gap, its 𝐪→𝟎\mathbf{q}\to\mathbf{0} dispersion has linear behavior (as seen in Fig. 2 (c))

ΩL−​(𝐪)=π​n2​D​|𝐪|​(1−e−|𝐪|​ts)=π​n2​D​ts​|𝐪|+O⁡(|𝐪|3/2)\displaystyle\Omega_{L}^{-}(\mathbf{q})=\sqrt{\pi n_{\rm 2D}|\mathbf{q}|(1-e^{-|\mathbf{q}|t_{s}})}=\sqrt{\pi n_{\rm 2D}t_{s}}|\mathbf{q}|+O(|\mathbf{q}|^{3/2}) (31)

with a divergent speed of sound, as ts→∞t_{s}\to\infty restoring the behavior of the 2D monolayer plasmon. As a gapless neutral mode, the optical plasmon constitutes a 2D Pines demon [52] in the quasicrystal spectrum.

Both for honeycomb and twisted configurations in the large ts/rst_{s}/r_{s} limit where the gap is small, we have the concavity inequality

ΩL−​(𝐪)+ΩL+​(𝐪)−2​ωL​(𝐪)≈π​n2​D​|𝐪|​(1−e−|𝐪|​ts)+π​n2​D​|𝐪|​(1+e−|𝐪|​ts)−2​π​n2​D​|𝐪|<0\displaystyle\Omega_{L}^{-}(\mathbf{q})+\Omega_{L}^{+}(\mathbf{q})-2\omega_{L}(\mathbf{q})\approx\sqrt{\pi n_{\rm 2D}|\mathbf{q}|(1-e^{-|\mathbf{q}|t_{s}})}+\sqrt{\pi n_{\rm 2D}|\mathbf{q}|(1+e^{-|\mathbf{q}|t_{s}})}-2\sqrt{\pi n_{\rm 2D}|\mathbf{q}|}<0 (32)

and the softening of the out of phase longitudinal mode is such that the ZPE is globally lowered relative to decoupled layers. This behavior is seen in Fig. S3(a)\,(a) for the large ts/rst_{s}/r_{s} dependence of the ZPE of both honeycomb and quasicrystal approximant. While the lowering of ZPE relative to the decoupled limit persists to lower ts/rst_{s}/r_{s} for the quasicrystal, the gap of the honeycomb stacking eventually becomes significant making the ZPE exceed the decoupled limit.

V Low ts/rst_{s}/r_{s} considerations

In this section, we comment on the low ts/rst_{s}/r_{s} behavior of the bilayer. Throughout, we have focused on the competition of various triangular stackings. Being the ground state of a monolayer Wigner crystal, triangular layers are favored when intralayer interaction dominates at large ts/rst_{s}/r_{s}. The mechanical stability of twisted triangular layers governs the allowed configurations of the system. Within the constraint of a given commensurate supercell, we find that twisted configuration become unstable and relax to honeycomb when interlayer interaction is sufficiently strong. In particular, the quasicrystal approximant at a 29.84∘29.84^{\circ} twist relaxes back to honeycomb for ts/rs≲1.95t_{s}/r_{s}\lesssim 1.95 which is out of the large ts/rst_{s}/r_{s} regions of interest of Fig. 3-4.

We proceed to summarize the features of the classical landscape first studied in [24]. As interlayer interaction is increased, unit cells sheared at an angle ϕ\phi between 𝐚1ℓ\mathbf{a}_{1}^{\ell} and 𝐚2ℓ\mathbf{a}_{2}^{\ell} start competing with the ϕ=60∘\phi=60^{\circ} honeycomb stacking. In Fig. S4, we obtain the minimal energy configuration for fixed unit cells with shear ϕ\phi for different ts/rst_{s}/r_{s}. In panel (a)(a), we show a ϕ\phi sweep at large ts/rst_{s}/r_{s} highlighting the global classical energy minimum at the honeycomb stacking. Then panel (b) shows that from ts/rs<1.835t_{s}/r_{s}<1.835, the classical ground state discontinuously becomes a sheared configuration disconnected from the honeycomb configuration. The shear angle ϕ\phi of this rhombic ground state is continuously increased as ts/rst_{s}/r_{s} is further reduced (see panel (c)(c)). Eventually, it reaches ϕ=90∘\phi=90^{\circ} at ts/rs=1.56t_{s}/r_{s}=1.56. Below this value, the staggered square ground state associated with this shear is the ground state of the system across all shears as can be seen in panel (d)(d). At even lower ts/rst_{s}/r_{s}, the bilayer crystal can lower its energy further by forming a staggered stacking of rectangles and finally, by becoming a monolayer triangular Wigner crystal. We point out that these phases are not accessible in a fully 3​D3D quantum well where the bilayer collapses to a monolayer at small well thickness [1].
